newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Trade unions group slams China for rights abuses.
newsitem.headline: Trade unions group slams China for rights abuses.

text.p: A new report on workers' rights in China says Beijing is systematically crushing all attempts to form trade unions and has detained dozens of activists on spurious charges.

"Search and Destroy", a report by the Brussels-based International Confederation of Free Trade Unions, says China daily violates fundamental human rights, adding there has been little improvement since the Tiananmen Square uprising of 1989.
"The persistent criminalisation of legitimate union activity ... confirms the authorities' long-standing policy of stamping out any independent trade union activity," the report says.

The ICFTU report is timed to coincide with the current session of the United Nations High Commission for Human Rights in Geneva, where Denmark is leading a bid for a resolution condemning China's record.

An attempt last week by Copenhagen to push for an European Union-sponsored resolution collapsed when France said recent improvements by China on human rights suggested dialogue was better than confrontation.

The EU divisions -- coupled with Washington's delay in deciding to co-sponsor the resolution until after last week's visit to China by U.S. Vice President Al Gore -- makes it unlikely the resolution will be adopted.
The ICFTU report is dedicated to Li Wenming, a trade union activist detained in Shenzhen since 1994.

Li, a former journalist who wrote about conditions faced by migrant workers in China's booming south, was tried in November on charges of conspiring to subvert the government but a verdict or sentence was never announced.

The ICFTU report lists 67 people with links to trade union organisations who have been detained, sent to forced labour camps or confined to mental hopsitals. Many of them need urgent medical attention.
It calls on China to ratify and implement various United Nations covenants covering human rights and labour activities as well as release activists detained without trial.
China said last week it would would sign the U.N. International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, but was silent on a similar pact on political freedoms.
Beijing's announcement was timed to coincide with a visit to China by French Defence Minister Charles Millon in a meeting on Monday.
France hailed the move and said it hoped a EU ban on arms sales to China imposed after the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown could be lifted.
Human rights activists have linked this and an enormous contract for French-built Airbus aircraft to China as reasons for France's reluctance to approve the resolution.
The U.S. human rights official in Geneva said the motion had at least 12 co-sponsors so far and Washington would lobby intensively in capitals worldwide to clinch crucial swing votes.
But he said China's delegation was expected to present its own "no-action motion" seeking to quash all debate on Tuesday when the 53 member states vote on the Western resolution.

Many Western diplomats and U.N. sources expect Beijing to escape formal censure for the seventh straight year at the six-week session. Last year 27 states voted in favour of China's no-action motion, 20 voted against with six abstentions.
